idiom_name: Polly retry strategy via Microsoft.Extensions.Http.Resilience handlers
implementation_notes: Retry in .NET is library work: Microsoft.Extensions.Http.Resilience (Polly underneath) attaches the policy to an HttpClient through the dependency-injection pipeline, so AddStandardResilienceHandler() yields a documented default - 3 retries with exponential backoff, jitter enabled and a 2 second base delay - wrapped in rate-limiter, total-timeout, circuit-breaker and per-attempt-timeout strategies, while AddResilienceHandler(...) lets you compose your own retry strategy. The classic hand-written loop is replaced by the handler pipeline: the decision moves out of the call site into RetryStrategyOptions and the request is retried inside the message handler, which is why calling code looks unchanged. The standard handler retries every HTTP method, so non-idempotent verbs must be excluded explicitly (Retry.DisableForUnsafeHttpMethods() or DisableFor(HttpMethod.Post, ...)); a hand-rolled loop is still justified for non-HTTP work such as database calls where no Polly pipeline is wired in.
pitfalls: Retrying unsafe HTTP methods by default duplicates side effects: the standard handler retries all verbs until DisableForUnsafeHttpMethods or DisableFor excludes them.
Stacking resilience handlers (or wrapping a Polly pipeline around a client that already has one) multiplies attempts; call RemoveAllResilienceHandlers before adding a custom pipeline.
An HttpClient built outside the DI pipeline does not receive the handler, and creating a new HttpClient per call exhausts sockets - use IHttpClientFactory.

The retry strategy only sees failures it handles (HttpRequestException, timeouts, the documented status codes); an exception thrown by your own deserialization code is not transient unless ShouldHandle says so.

Handler timeouts interact: the standard pipeline's total timeout (30 seconds by default) bounds the whole retry sequence, so a short total timeout silently reduces the number of attempts that can actually run.
